title: Disaster Risk Management and Recovery
subtitle: Rank your real local hazards, build a tested household plan and kit, and lead your community through warning, response and safer recovery.
description: A practical course for women who hold households and communities together when floods, fires, windstorms or droughts strike. You will use Nigerian forecasts and local memory to rank your risks, build and test a kit, plan and phone tree, and learn safe first steps and build-back-better recovery.
outcomes: Rank your household's hazards using official NiMet and NIHSA outlooks, local history and a likelihood x impact score
Audit household readiness on a 40-point checklist and turn gaps into a dated action list
Assemble a 3-day emergency kit and grab bag using correct water and food quantities
Write, rehearse and time a one-page household evacuation plan that includes every vulnerable member
Set up and test a community phone tree and track readiness with clear indicators
Return home safely, make water safe, record losses and plan a build-back-better recovery
audience: Women who manage households, small businesses or community groups in flood-, fire- or drought-prone areas and want to lead practical preparedness.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp and a calculator
A notebook and pen, or Google Sheets
Zip bags or a waterproof pouch for document copies
A torch, whistle and power bank for the grab bag

modules.title: Understanding Disaster Risk Where You Live
modules.overview: Disasters are not just bad luck. In this module you learn how hazards turn into disasters, how to read the real risks in your own area using official Nigerian warnings and local memory, and how to audit your household honestly so you know exactly what to fix first.

lessons.title: How a Hazard Becomes a Disaster: Risk, Exposure, Vulnerability and the Management Cycle
objectives: Explain the difference between a hazard and a disaster in plain words
Break any risk into hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity
Name the four stages of the disaster management cycle and what happens in each
Use the risk idea to compare two households facing the same event

blocks.text: Heavy rain is not a disaster. A dry season is not a disaster. These are **hazards**: natural or human-made events that *could* cause harm. A hazard only becomes a **disaster** when it hits people and property that are exposed and not able to cope, so that normal life breaks down and people need outside help. This is the way the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) defines the words, and it changes how we think. If disaster depends on people and their situation, then people can reduce it.

blocks.name: cloud-with-rain
blocks.alt: A rain cloud with falling rain
blocks.caption: Rain is a hazard; whether it becomes a disaster depends on exposure, vulnerability and preparation.

blocks.text: The four parts of disaster risk

Disaster professionals describe risk with a simple idea: **risk grows with hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and shrinks with capacity**. You do not need a formula to use it. You only need to ask four questions about your own home.

head: Part
Plain meaning
Question to ask at home
rows: Hazard
The event that can cause harm: flood, drought, fire, windstorm, disease outbreak
What events have happened here before, and how often?
Exposure
People, homes, goods and income that sit in the hazard's path
Is my house, shop or farm in a low area, near a river bank, or near a drainage channel?
Vulnerability
Conditions that make harm worse
Who in my house cannot move fast? Are my documents and savings easily destroyed?
Capacity
Skills, plans, savings and relationships that help you cope
Do we have a plan, a kit, some cash and neighbours we can call?

blocks.text: Notice that you cannot stop the rain, but you can work on the other three. You can raise goods off the floor (less exposure), keep documents in a waterproof bag (less vulnerability), and build a plan and a small emergency fund (more capacity). This is the heart of **disaster risk management**: reducing the harm before the hazard arrives, responding well when it comes, and recovering in a way that leaves you safer than before.
The disaster management cycle

blocks.title: The disaster management cycle
items: Mitigation: reduce the risk
Preparedness: plan and equip
Response: act to save lives
Recovery: rebuild safer
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next, and lessons from recovery should strengthen mitigation before the next event.

items: **Mitigation** means lowering the risk itself: clearing drains before the rains, not building on a flood plain, raising a shop floor, keeping a firebreak around a compound in harmattan.
**Preparedness** means getting ready for what you cannot prevent: an emergency kit, an evacuation plan, a warning system, practice drills.
**Response** covers the hours and days during and just after the event: moving to safety, first aid, finding family members, getting clean water.
**Recovery** covers the weeks and months after: cleaning, repairing, restarting income, and rebuilding in a stronger way.

blocks.text: The cycle matters because most people only think about disasters during the response stage, when it is already too late to do the cheap and simple things. A drain cleared in April costs a few hours of community work. A house flooded in September can cost a family years of savings.
The global framework, in brief

In 2015, countries including Nigeria adopted the **Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015 to 2030**. It sets four priorities: understand disaster risk; strengthen how risk is governed; invest in risk reduction for resilience; and improve preparedness for effective response, with the aim to **"Build Back Better"** in recovery. This course follows the same order at household and community level: understand your risk (Module 1), prepare (Module 2), then respond, recover and lead (Module 3).

blocks.title: Worked example: same flood, two different outcomes
blocks.context: For example, Amina and Grace live on the same street in a low part of town. One night heavy rain floods the street to knee height.
steps: Hazard: the same for both, the same rain and the same water level.
Exposure: Amina keeps her provisions stock on wooden pallets about 50 cm above the floor; Grace keeps hers in sacks on the floor.
Vulnerability: Amina's NIN slip, land papers and school certificates are in a zip bag on a high shelf; Grace's are in a drawer near the floor.
Capacity: Amina has a written plan, a torch, a charged power bank and the phone numbers of two neighbours on higher ground. Grace has none of these.

Amina wakes the children, switches off the mains at the meter while the floor is still dry, and moves the family to her neighbour's house in 10 minutes. Grace searches in the dark and loses her documents and most of her stock.
blocks.result: The hazard was identical. The difference in harm came from exposure, vulnerability and capacity, which are the parts a household can change.

blocks.title: Women carry a heavy share
blocks.text: In many Nigerian homes women are responsible for children, older relatives, food stores and often a small business. That means women are both at higher risk and often best placed to lead preparation. A plan built by the person who actually manages the home is usually the most realistic plan.

Throughout this course you will build one real product: a **household and community readiness file**. By the end it will contain your risk ranking, an audit, a kit list, a written plan, a drill record, a recovery checklist and a 90-day plan for your community.

takeaways: A hazard becomes a disaster only when exposed, vulnerable people cannot cope.
You cannot stop most hazards, but you can reduce exposure and vulnerability and increase capacity.
The cycle is mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery; cheap actions happen before the event.
The Sendai Framework's priorities run from understanding risk to building back better.

activity.title: Map your four risk parts
steps: Write the four headings Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability and Capacity on one page of a notebook.
Under Hazard, list every event your household has experienced or heard of on your street in the last 10 years.
Under Exposure and Vulnerability, write at least three honest points each about your home and family.
Under Capacity, write what you already have: savings, skills, contacts, a plan or none.
Circle one item in Exposure or Vulnerability you could change this month.
activity.evidence: A photo of the completed four-part page with one circled action.

lessons.title: Reading Your Local Hazards: Nigerian Warnings, Community Memory and a Risk Ranking
objectives: Identify the main hazards affecting Nigerian communities and their warning signs
Find official seasonal outlooks from NiMet and NIHSA and the emergency agencies NEMA, SEMA and LEMA
Gather local disaster history through a short community interview
Rank your hazards with a simple likelihood and impact score

blocks.text: Good preparation starts with the right hazard. A family in a riverside community in Kogi or Bayelsa needs a different plan from a family in a dry northern village or in a crowded Lagos market area. In this lesson you combine two kinds of knowledge: **official forecasts** and **local memory**, then rank what you find.
Common hazards and their early signs

head: Hazard
Where it often hits
Early signs to watch
rows: River flooding
Communities along the Niger, Benue and their tributaries, and low-lying areas downstream of dams
Official flood outlooks, rising river levels upstream, news of dam water releases, many days of heavy rain
Flash and urban flooding
Towns with blocked drains, homes built on waterways
Very heavy rain in a short time, drains already full, water collecting fast on roads
Drought and dry spells
Mainly northern states, but dry spells also affect farms further south
Late onset of rains, long breaks between rains, wells dropping early
Fire
Markets, crowded compounds, homes with gas cylinders or generators, dry bush in harmattan
Overloaded sockets, gas smell, dry grass near houses, open burning
Windstorm
Many areas at the start of the rainy season
Sudden strong winds before rain, loose roofing sheets
Disease outbreak after floods
Areas with flooded wells and toilets
Dirty water in wells, many cases of watery diarrhoea

blocks.name: weather-forecast
blocks.alt: A woman checking a large weather forecast display
blocks.caption: Official seasonal forecasts tell you what kind of season to prepare for before it starts.

blocks.text: Where official warnings come from

items: **NiMet (Nigerian Meteorological Agency)** publishes a Seasonal Climate Prediction early each year with expected onset and end of rains, and dry spell risk by area, plus daily and short-range weather warnings.
**NIHSA (Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency)** publishes an Annual Flood Outlook that names states and local government areas at high, moderate and low flood risk.

**NEMA (National Emergency Management Agency)** coordinates disaster response nationally. Each state has a **SEMA** (State Emergency Management Agency), and many local governments have a **LEMA** or local emergency committee. These are the offices that issue alerts, run evacuations and register affected people for relief.
**112** is Nigeria's toll-free national emergency number for police, fire and ambulance calls.

blocks.text: These outlooks are usually reported on radio, TV and online news. A simple habit is to search "NIHSA flood outlook" and your state name each year when it is released, and write down whether your local government area is listed. Many state agencies also share alerts on their social media pages.

blocks.title: Check the source before you share
blocks.text: Fake flood and dam alerts circulate on WhatsApp every rainy season. Before forwarding a warning, check that it comes from NiMet, NIHSA, NEMA, your SEMA or a trusted news outlet. Spreading false alarms makes people ignore real ones.
Local memory: the community interview

Official maps are broad. Older residents know which street floods first, how high the water reached, and what happened before it came. Spend 20 minutes with two or three elders, a market women's leader or a long-time landlord. Ask: What events have happened here, and in which years? How high did the water go, or how long did the drought last? What signs came before? What helped people, and what did not? Write the answers down; this becomes your community's disaster history.
Ranking your hazards

Give each hazard two scores from 1 (low) to 5 (high). **Likelihood**: how often it happens here. **Impact**: how badly it would hurt your household. Multiply them to get a **priority score** out of 25. Then plan seriously for the highest one first.

blocks.title: Hazard priority matrix
items: Rare but severe: plan and insure
Likely and severe: act now
Rare and mild: watch
Likely but mild: simple fixes
blocks.caption: Hazards in the top-right box get your first time and money.

blocks.title: Worked example: ranking hazards for one household
blocks.context: For example, Halima lives in a bungalow in Makurdi, about 400 metres from the Benue river, and sells foodstuff from a shop in front of her house.
steps: River flood: it reached her street in 2012 and 2022 according to her neighbours, and her LGA appears in the flood outlook. Likelihood 4, impact 5. Score 4 x 5 = 20.
House fire: she cooks with a gas cylinder and runs a generator. No fire in her compound so far. Likelihood 2, impact 5. Score 2 x 5 = 10.
Windstorm: roofing sheets have lifted on two houses nearby. Likelihood 3, impact 2. Score 3 x 2 = 6.
Dry spell: affects food prices but not her house directly. Likelihood 3, impact 2. Score 6.
She sorts the scores: flood 20, fire 10, windstorm 6, dry spell 6.
blocks.result: Flood is her top priority, so her kit, plan and drills will be built around flooding first, with fire safety as the second focus.

blocks.text: Do not stop at one hazard forever. Once your top hazard is covered, add the second. But a household that is truly ready for its main hazard is far safer than one that knows a little about everything.

takeaways: Match your plan to your real local hazard, not a general list.
NiMet's Seasonal Climate Prediction and NIHSA's Annual Flood Outlook tell you what season to expect.
NEMA, SEMA and LEMA coordinate response; 112 is the national emergency number.
Elders and long-time residents hold detailed local history that maps miss.
Score likelihood x impact out of 25 and plan for the top hazard first.

activity.title: Build your hazard ranking
steps: Look up this year's NIHSA flood outlook and NiMet seasonal prediction for your state on the news or online, and note what they say for your area.
Interview at least two long-time residents using the four questions in this lesson.
List four hazards and score each for likelihood and impact from 1 to 5.
Multiply the scores, sort from highest to lowest, and write your top hazard in large letters at the top of the page.
Save the phone number of your SEMA or local emergency office and 112 in your phone.
activity.evidence: Interview notes and a ranked hazard table with scores.

lessons.title: Auditing Household Readiness: A Scored Checklist and Your Gap List
objectives: Score your household's readiness across supplies, plans, documents, people and money
Calculate a readiness percentage and compare it later
Turn the gaps you find into a short, ordered action list
Check community readiness with five simple questions

blocks.text: Many families believe they are "somehow ready". An audit replaces that feeling with facts. It takes about 30 minutes, it costs nothing, and it gives you a baseline number you can improve and measure. The aim is not to feel bad. The aim is an accurate list of what to fix, in the right order.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A written, scored checklist turns vague worry into a clear list of tasks.

blocks.text: The 20-point household audit
Score each item: **2** if it is fully in place and checked in the last six months, **1** if it is partly there, **0** if it is missing. The maximum score is 40.

head: Area
Audit items (score 0, 1 or 2 each)
rows: Water and food

1. Stored drinking water for at least 3 days. 2. Non-perishable food for 3 days. 3. A way to make water safe (boiling fuel, or bleach with known strength). 4. Food and water checked for expiry in the last 6 months.
Light, power, communication
5. Torch with working batteries or a rechargeable lamp. 6. Power bank kept charged. 7. Key phone numbers written on paper, not only in the phone. 8. A radio or reliable way to receive warnings.
Documents and money

9. Copies of NIN, birth certificates, land or tenancy papers in a waterproof bag. 10. Photos of the same documents stored online or with a trusted relative. 11. Some emergency cash at home. 12. Emergency savings you can reach quickly.
Health and safety

13. A basic first aid kit. 14. A list of regular medicines for each family member and a few days' supply. 15. A working fire extinguisher or sand bucket near the kitchen. 16. Everyone knows how to switch off gas and electricity.
People and plan

17. A written plan with a meeting point and safe destination. 18. Every family member, including children, can explain the plan. 19. A named helper for each person who needs help to move. 20. The plan has been practised at least once.

blocks.title: Five areas of household readiness
items: Water and food
Light and communication
Documents and money
Health and safety
People and plan
blocks.caption: A gap in any one area can undo the others, so the audit checks all five.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring and reading the result
blocks.context: For example, Chioma, a hairdresser in Port Harcourt, does the audit with her husband and their 12-year-old son on a Sunday afternoon.
steps: Water and food: they have some sachet water and garri but nothing planned. Items 1 to 4 score 1, 1, 1, 0 = 3.
Light and communication: torch works, power bank is usually charged, numbers are only in phones, they have a radio. Scores 2, 1, 0, 2 = 5.
Documents and money: originals are in a cupboard, no copies, a little cash, savings are in an ajo group paid out once a month. Scores 0, 0, 1, 1 = 2.
Health and safety: small first aid box, medicine list not written, no extinguisher, only the husband knows the gas valve. Scores 1, 0, 0, 1 = 2.
People and plan: no written plan. Items 17 to 20 score 0, 0, 0, 0 = 0.
Total: 3 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 12 out of 40. Readiness = 12 / 40 x 100 = 30%.
blocks.result: Chioma's household is 30% ready. The weakest areas are People and plan (0 of 8) and Documents and money (2 of 8), so those become the first actions.

blocks.text: From gaps to an action list

Now sort every item that scored 0 or 1 into three groups. **Free and fast**: things you can do today, like writing phone numbers on paper or showing everyone the gas valve. **Low cost**: things that need a small purchase, like a zip bag for documents or a torch. **Takes time**: things that need saving or the whole family, like building an emergency fund or running a drill. Do all the free ones this week. Schedule the low-cost ones by date. Put the time-heavy ones into your plan for the next modules.

blocks.title: Audit with the whole household
blocks.text: Ask children and older relatives to answer items 16 and 18 themselves. If your mother-in-law cannot say where the family meets, the plan is not yet real, even if it is written down.
Five questions about your community

items: Is there any warning method for our main hazard, official or informal, and has it been tested?
Is there a known safe gathering point on higher or safer ground?
Does anyone keep a list of older, disabled or sick residents who would need help?
Do we know the contact for our LEMA, SEMA or local emergency committee?
Are drains, firebreaks or other shared protections maintained, and by whom?

blocks.text: A "no" to any of these is not a failure. It is a starting point for the community work in Module 3. Keep your audit sheet; you will score it again at the end of the course and compare.

takeaways: Score 20 items at 0, 1 or 2 for a baseline out of 40 and a percentage.
The five areas are water and food, light and communication, documents and money, health and safety, and people and plan.
Sort gaps into free and fast, low cost, and takes time, then act on the free ones this week.
A plan only counts if everyone, including children and elders, can explain it.

activity.title: Complete your baseline audit
steps: Copy the 20 audit items into your notebook or a Google Sheet.
Score each item with your household present and add up the total out of 40.
Calculate your readiness percentage: total divided by 40, times 100.
Sort every 0 and 1 item into free and fast, low cost, or takes time.
Complete at least two free and fast items within 7 days and tick them off.
Answer the five community questions in writing.
activity.evidence: The dated audit sheet with total, percentage, sorted gap list and two ticked actions.

quiz.q: Two neighbours face the same storm. One loses everything and one loses very little. According to this course, what explains the difference?
options: The hazard was stronger at one house
Differences in exposure, vulnerability and capacity
Pure luck, since disasters cannot be planned for
Only the quality of the roof
quiz.explain: The hazard was the same. Harm depends on how exposed and vulnerable each household was and how much capacity it had to cope.

quiz.q: Clearing blocked drains before the rainy season belongs to which stage of the disaster management cycle?
quiz.explain: Mitigation reduces the risk itself before the event. Clearing drains lowers the chance and depth of flooding.

quiz.q: Ngozi wants to know if her local government area is at high flood risk this year. Which source is designed for this?
quiz.explain: The Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency publishes an Annual Flood Outlook naming states and LGAs by flood risk level.

quiz.q: Fatima scores fire as likelihood 2 and impact 5, and windstorm as likelihood 4 and impact 2. Which should she plan for first?
options: Windstorm, because it is more likely
Fire, with a score of 10 against 8
quiz.explain: 2 x 5 = 10 for fire and 4 x 2 = 8 for windstorm. The higher priority score goes first.

quiz.q: A household audit totals 18 out of 40. What is the readiness percentage?
After her audit, Esther finds that only she knows the family meeting point. What is the best next step?
options: Explain and walk the meeting point with every household member, then ask each to repeat it
Write it in her phone notes
Wait until the rainy season to tell them
quiz.explain: A plan is only real when every member, including children and elders, can explain it. Walking the route together is free and fast.

modules.title: Preparedness in Practice: Kits, Plans, Drills and Early Warning
modules.overview: This module turns your audit into real protection. You will calculate and assemble an emergency kit and grab bag, write and rehearse a household plan that includes everyone, and help set up and test a simple community early warning system with clear measures of progress.

lessons.title: Building an Emergency Kit and Grab Bag: Quantities, Costs and Upkeep
objectives: Calculate water and food quantities for your household for 3 days
Pack a grab bag with documents, cash, light, medicines and communication
Plan the kit purchase in stages to fit a tight budget
Set up a simple routine to keep the kit fresh

blocks.text: An emergency kit has two parts. The **home kit** keeps your household going for at least three days if you are cut off at home or come back to a damaged home. The **grab bag** (also called a go bag) is a small, ready-packed bag you can pick up in under a minute if you must leave. The Ready.gov guidance from the United States emergency agency recommends water of about one gallon (roughly 4 litres) per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation, and a several-day supply of non-perishable food. We use 3 days as the minimum.

blocks.name: package
blocks.caption: Keep the home kit together in one box or bucket, not scattered around the house.

blocks.text: Priorities: what matters most

blocks.title: Emergency kit priorities
items: Water and safe-water method
Documents, phone and cash
Medicines and first aid
Light and communication
Food that needs no cooking
Comfort and hygiene items
blocks.caption: Fill the kit from the top of this list down, so the most critical items are there first even if money runs short.

blocks.text: Calculating water and food

blocks.title: Worked example: a 3-day kit for a family of six
blocks.context: For example, Blessing lives in Lokoja with her husband, three children and her elderly mother: six people in total.
steps: Water: 6 people x 4 litres x 3 days = 72 litres. She uses three 25-litre jerrycans with tight lids, which hold 75 litres.
She labels each jerrycan with the date filled and plans to empty and refill them every 3 months.

Food: she plans 2 simple meals a day for 6 people for 3 days = 36 meal portions, using foods that need little or no cooking: garri, groundnuts, sealed tins of sardines and beans, biscuits, dried fruit and sugar.
She buys tins with ring-pull lids so no can opener is needed, and stores everything in a covered plastic drum off the floor.
Medicines: her mother takes daily blood pressure tablets, so she asks the pharmacist how to keep a few days' extra supply and writes the medicine name and prescriber on a card in the grab bag.
blocks.result: Blessing's home kit covers 72 litres of water and 36 meal portions, plus a written medicine card, enough for her household to manage 3 days without outside help.

blocks.text: What goes in the grab bag

head: Item
Why it matters
Tip
rows: Copies of NIN slips, birth certificates, land or tenancy papers, school certificates
Needed to register for relief, reclaim property, re-enrol children
Seal in two zip bags; keep originals in a safe place, photos online
Paper list of phone numbers
Phones die or get lost
Include family, neighbours, SEMA or LEMA, 112, nearest clinic
Cash in small notes
POS and bank apps may be down for days
Agree an amount you can afford to keep aside
Charged power bank and charger
Warnings, calls and mobile money
Recharge it monthly
Torch with spare batteries, whistle
Light and calling for help
A whistle carries further than a voice
Medicines, medicine card, basic first aid items
Health problems do not pause in emergencies
Bandages, plasters, gloves, clean cloth, oral rehydration salts sachets
Sanitary pads, a change of clothes, a wrapper, baby items
Dignity and hygiene for women, girls and babies
Pack for every person, not only adults
Two bottles of water and snacks
The first hours on the move
Rotate with the home kit

blocks.title: Store water and food safely
blocks.text: Use clean, food-grade containers with lids, never containers that held fuel, kerosene or chemicals. Keep them off the floor, out of direct sun and away from fuel and cleaning products. Check tins for swelling, rust or dents and throw away any that are damaged.
Building the kit on a budget

You do not need to buy everything at once. Prices vary by market, so collect your own prices. A practical approach is a **four-week build**: week 1, documents copied and sealed plus a paper phone list (almost free); week 2, water containers filled; week 3, torch, whistle and power bank; week 4, food and first aid items. Many women build it through their savings group by agreeing that each member buys one item per week.

Money is part of preparedness too. A small emergency fund, even saved weekly in an ajo or esusu group or a separate savings account with a regulated bank or mobile money provider, gives you options after an event. Keep a little cash in the grab bag and the rest somewhere you can reach quickly but safely.
Keeping the kit alive

items: Write a kit list on paper and tape it to the kit box with the date of the last check.
Every 3 months: empty and refill water, test the torch, recharge the power bank, check food dates and use up items close to expiry.
Before the rainy season or harmattan: check document copies, medicines and the phone list are up to date.
After you use anything from the kit, replace it within the week.

takeaways: Plan at least 4 litres of water per person per day for 3 days: people x 4 x 3.
The grab bag holds document copies, phone list, cash, power bank, torch, whistle, medicines and hygiene items.
Store water only in clean food-grade containers, never ones that held fuel or chemicals.
Build the kit in four weekly steps and check it every 3 months.

activity.title: Assemble your kit in stages
steps: Calculate your household's water need: number of people x 4 litres x 3 days.
Copy and seal your key documents in two zip bags and write a paper phone list this week.
Fill and date your water containers.
Pack the grab bag using the table in this lesson and tick off each item.
Tape a kit list with the next check date to the kit box.
activity.evidence: Photos of the home kit and grab bag with the dated kit list visible, plus your water calculation.

lessons.title: Writing and Rehearsing a Household Plan That Includes Everyone
objectives: Write a one-page household emergency plan for your top hazard
Assign a named helper for every child, older person, pregnant woman or person with disability
Give correct first actions for flood, gas leak, fire and generator fumes
Run and time an evacuation drill and improve the result

blocks.text: A plan is a set of decisions made calmly, in advance, so nobody has to think clearly in the dark while water is rising or smoke is filling a room. The best household plans fit on **one page**, are written in the language everyone in the house speaks, and are practised.

blocks.name: route-planning
blocks.alt: A person planning a route on a map
blocks.caption: Choose your routes and meeting points before the event, and walk them with the whole family.

blocks.text: The seven parts of a one-page plan

items: **Trigger**: what makes you act. For example, an official flood alert for your LGA, water entering the compound, or a fire alarm.
**Safe destination**: where you go. A relative or friend on higher ground, a school or church the community uses, or an official camp named by SEMA.
**Two routes**: a main route and a second one in case the first is blocked, both checked on foot.
**Meeting points**: one just outside the home (for fire) and one away from the area (if family members are separated).
**Roles**: who takes the grab bag, who switches off gas and electricity, who helps each person who needs help.
**Contacts**: one out-of-town contact everyone calls or messages to say "I am safe", so the family can be traced.
**Return rule**: you return only when authorities say it is safe and an adult has checked the house.

blocks.text: Planning for those who need more help

General plans often fail the people most at risk. Go through your household one person at a time. A baby needs a carrier and supplies. A child needs to know the meeting point and the out-of-town contact number by heart. An older relative may walk slowly or need help with steps. A pregnant woman may tire quickly and should know where the nearest health facility is. A person who uses a wheelchair, crutches or hearing aid needs those items packed and a route they can actually use. Give each of these people a **named helper** and a **back-up helper**. In the community, the same idea becomes a list of residents who need help, kept privately by a trusted person.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: Lists of people with disabilities or illnesses are sensitive. Ask permission, record only what helpers need to know, and share the list only with the people who will act on it.
First actions for common emergencies

head: Situation
Do
Do not
rows: Flood warning or rising water
Move people to higher ground early; switch off electricity at the mains only if you are dry and the floor is dry; take the grab bag
Walk or drive through moving water: about 15 cm of moving water can knock you down and about 30 cm can sweep a vehicle away
Smell of cooking gas
Close the cylinder valve if safe, open doors and windows, get everyone out, call for help from outside
Switch lights or anything electrical on or off, use a phone near the leak, or light a flame
Fire in the home
Shout to alert everyone, get out low under smoke, close doors behind you, meet at the outside meeting point, call 112
Go back inside for belongings; throw water on burning oil or electrical fires
Clothes on fire
Stop, drop to the ground, cover the face and roll
Run, which feeds the flames
Running a generator
Place it outdoors, well away from doors and windows
Run it inside a room, corridor, garage or shop, even with a window open: its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill sleeping people

blocks.title: Using a fire extinguisher: P.A.S.S.
blocks.text: Only fight a small fire with a clear exit behind you. Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side. If the fire grows or the room fills with smoke, leave immediately and close the door.

blocks.title: Flood evacuation sequence
items: Warning or trigger
Wake everyone, assign helpers
Grab bag, switch off power
Leave by main route
Meet and count heads
Message out-of-town contact
blocks.caption: Practising this exact order is what makes it automatic at night.

blocks.text: Running a drill

blocks.title: Worked example: timing and improving a drill
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ibadan runs a flood drill with her household of five, including her father who uses a walking stick, on a Saturday evening.
steps: She starts a timer on her phone and says "Flood alert, go".

First drill result: 9 minutes 40 seconds to reach the neighbour's house on higher ground, about 300 metres away. Problems: the torch was in a different room, nobody knew who would carry the grab bag, and her father's shoes were not by the door.
Fixes: torch hung by the door, her eldest son named as grab bag carrier, her husband named as her father's helper, her father's shoes and stick kept by his bed.
Second drill a week later: 5 minutes 50 seconds.
Improvement: 9 min 40 s = 580 seconds; 5 min 50 s = 350 seconds; 580 - 350 = 230 seconds saved, about 40% faster (230 / 580 = 0.40).
blocks.result: Two short drills and three free fixes made the family's evacuation about 40% faster, and everyone now knows their role.

blocks.text: Practise at least twice a year: before the rainy season and before harmattan. Each time, write the date, the time taken and what you changed.

takeaways: A good plan fits on one page: trigger, destination, two routes, meeting points, roles, contacts, return rule.
Give every person who needs help a named helper and a back-up.
Never walk through moving floodwater, never run a generator indoors, and never touch switches when you smell gas.
Time your drills, fix what slowed you, and drill again.

activity.title: Write and test your plan
steps: Write a one-page plan with all seven parts for your top hazard.
Name a helper and a back-up for each child, older person, pregnant woman or person with disability in your home.
Walk both routes to your safe destination with the family.
Run a timed drill, list what slowed you down, and fix at least two things.
Run a second timed drill within two weeks and calculate the improvement.
activity.evidence: The signed one-page plan and a drill record showing both times and the fixes made.

lessons.title: Community Early Warning and Measuring Readiness
objectives: Describe the four elements of a people-centred early warning system
Design a phone tree and calculate how fast it can reach every household
Choose clear indicators to measure household and community readiness
Run an after-action review after a drill or real event

blocks.text: A warning is only useful if it reaches people in time and they know what to do. International bodies such as the World Meteorological Organization and UNDRR describe four elements of a **people-centred early warning system**. All four must work; a perfect forecast that nobody hears saves no one.

blocks.title: Four elements of early warning
items: Know the risk
Monitor and forecast
Spread the warning
Respond in time
blocks.caption: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link: knowledge, monitoring, communication and readiness to act.

items: **Risk knowledge**: your hazard ranking, community history and the list of people who need help (Module 1).
**Monitoring and forecasting**: NiMet and NIHSA forecasts, SEMA alerts, plus local watching, such as a marked pole by the river or drain showing danger levels.
**Warning dissemination and communication**: getting the message to every household fast, in the right language, through more than one channel.
**Preparedness and response capability**: households that have kits, plans and practised drills (the rest of this module).

blocks.text: A simple local danger marker

Official forecasts cover a whole state or river basin. A local marker tells your street when the danger is close. Choose a fixed point the warning lead can see safely, such as a concrete pole, bridge pillar or wall near the river or main drain. Using the flood marks elders showed you, paint three bands: **green** for normal levels, **yellow** for "get ready, check grab bags and move valuables up", and **red** for "move people to the safe destination now". Agree in a community meeting what each colour means, so the warning lead is acting on a shared rule, not a personal guess. Check the marker after each rainy season and repaint if needed. Never send anyone to read a marker in moving water or after dark during a storm.

blocks.name: public-address-loudspeaker
blocks.caption: Use more than one channel: phone tree, WhatsApp, loudspeaker, mosque or church announcement, town crier.

blocks.text: Designing a phone tree

A phone tree passes one message quickly by giving each person a small number of calls to make. The **warning lead** receives an official alert or sees the danger level, confirms it is genuine, and calls a few **street captains**. Each captain calls a fixed list of households. Calls matter because many people do not read WhatsApp messages at night, and some residents have basic phones. WhatsApp groups and voice notes in local languages are a useful second channel.

blocks.title: Worked example: how fast can 60 households be warned?
blocks.context: For example, a women's group in a riverside community in Kogi wants to warn 60 households. Each call takes about 1 minute including repeating the message.
steps: Option A: one person calls all 60 households. Time: 60 x 1 minute = 60 minutes.
Option B: the warning lead calls 5 street captains (5 minutes). Each captain calls 12 households (12 minutes), all at the same time.
Option B total: 5 + 12 = 17 minutes.
Option C: the lead calls 6 captains (6 minutes); each captain calls 10 households (10 minutes). Total 16 minutes, with one more captain to train.
They choose option B and name a back-up for each captain in case a phone is off.
blocks.result: Splitting the calls cuts warning time from about 60 minutes to about 17 minutes, a saving of 43 minutes that could mean leaving before the water rises.

blocks.title: Keep the message short and clear
blocks.text: A good warning says who it is from, what is happening, where, and what to do now. For example: "From the street committee: SEMA flood alert for our area tonight. Move children and elderly to the school on the hill now. Take your grab bag."
Measuring readiness honestly
Measuring stops a community from assuming it is ready. Choose a few indicators, record a starting value (baseline), set a target and check again on a fixed date.

head: Indicator
How to measure
Baseline example
Target example
rows: Households with a written plan
Street captains ask each household
30 of 60 (50%) in 3 months
Households with a 3-day water store
Quick visit or self-report
Phone tree reach time
Timed test message
Not tested
Under 20 minutes
Residents needing help with a named helper
Private list kept by a trusted person
0 of 9
9 of 9
Average household audit score
Repeat the 40-point audit

blocks.text: Percentages help compare progress: 8 of 60 is 8 / 60 x 100 = 13%. If 30 of 60 have plans after three months, that is 50%, an increase of 37 percentage points.
After-action review

After every drill, test message or real event, even a small flood that only filled the road, meet for 30 minutes and ask four questions: What did we expect to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we change, who will do it, and by when? Write the answers in a community record book with the date. Over the years this book becomes valuable local history.

blocks.title: Do not over-warn
blocks.text: Send a warning only when it is confirmed from an official source or a clear local danger sign. Always label tests clearly as tests. Too many false alarms make people ignore the real one.

takeaways: Early warning needs four links: risk knowledge, monitoring, communication and readiness to respond.
A phone tree with captains cuts warning time sharply; always name back-ups.
Use more than one channel, including calls and local-language voice notes.
Track a few indicators with a baseline and target, and run an after-action review after every test or event.

activity.title: Set up and test a mini phone tree
steps: Agree with at least 3 neighbours to act as street captains for 8 to 15 households each.
Write the call lists, the back-ups and a short template warning message.
Send a clearly labelled test message and time how long it takes to reach every household.
Record two readiness indicators with a baseline and a 3-month target.
Hold a 30-minute after-action review and write the four answers in a record book.
activity.evidence: The phone tree chart, the timed test result and the after-action review notes.

quiz.q: Grace's household has 5 people. Using 4 litres per person per day, how much water does she need for 3 days?
quiz.explain: 5 people x 4 litres x 3 days = 60 litres. Three 25-litre jerrycans would cover it with some to spare.

quiz.q: Which container is NOT suitable for storing emergency drinking water?
options: A clean food-grade jerrycan with a lid
A jerrycan that once held kerosene, rinsed with water
A new plastic drum with a tight cover
quiz.explain: Containers that held fuel or chemicals can contaminate water even after rinsing. Use only clean food-grade containers.

quiz.q: Kemi smells cooking gas strongly in her kitchen at night. What should she do first?
options: Switch on the light to find the leak
Light a match to check where it is coming from
Call from her phone while standing next to the cylinder
Close the valve if safe, open doors and windows, and get everyone out without touching switches
quiz.explain: Any spark, including a light switch or flame, can ignite gas. Ventilate, close the valve if safe, leave, and call from outside.

quiz.q: Water is flowing across the road between Aisha's family and the safe destination, about knee deep. What should they do?
options: Use the second route or wait on higher ground; never cross moving water
Send the strongest person first to test it
quiz.explain: About 15 cm of moving water can knock a person down and about 30 cm can sweep a vehicle away. That is why every plan needs a second route.

quiz.q: A drill took 600 seconds the first time and 420 seconds the second time. How much faster was the second drill?

A community has one person calling 40 households at 1 minute per call. They switch to 4 captains, each calling 10 households, after the lead calls the captains. Roughly how long does the new tree take?
quiz.explain: The lead takes about 4 minutes to call 4 captains, then the captains call 10 households each at the same time: 4 + 10 = 14 minutes.

modules.title: Response, Recovery and Community Leadership
modules.overview: When an event happens, the first days decide how fast a family recovers. This module covers safe return and safe water after a flood or fire, supporting people in distress, restarting income and building back better, and finally leading your community through partnerships and a 90-day readiness plan.

lessons.title: The First Days After: Safe Return, Safe Water and Psychological First Aid
objectives: Follow a safe sequence for returning to a home after flood or fire
Make water safe by boiling or with household bleach of known strength
Apply food safety rules to food touched by floodwater
Support a distressed neighbour using Look, Listen and Link

blocks.text: Many injuries and illnesses happen **after** the water goes down or the fire is out: electric shocks, collapsing walls, and diarrhoeal diseases from dirty water and spoiled food. Recovery must start safely. This lesson gives you a practical order of work for the first days.

blocks.title: The first two weeks after a flood
items: Day 0: safety and headcount
Days 1 to 3: water and food
Days 3 to 7: clean and dry
Week 2: repair and restart
blocks.caption: Doing things in this order prevents the second wave of harm that often follows the first.

blocks.text: Returning home safely

items: Return only when SEMA, LEMA or local leaders say the area is safe, and in daylight.
Look from outside first: cracks in walls, a sagging roof, a leaning building or a smell of gas mean do not enter. Ask for a check by a builder or the authorities.
Do not switch on electricity until a qualified electrician has checked the wiring, sockets and meter, especially if water reached them.
Wear closed shoes and gloves. Floodwater can hide broken glass, nails, snakes and sewage.
Take photos and videos of all damage before you clean or throw anything away. You will need them for relief registration, landlords or insurance (Lesson 3.2).
For fire damage, do not touch burnt electrical items or stay in a room with smoke or a strong smell.

blocks.name: potable-water-symbol
blocks.alt: A tap with a drinking glass symbol
blocks.caption: Treat all water as unsafe after a flood until it has been boiled or disinfected.

blocks.text: Making water safe

After flooding, wells, boreholes and tanks are often contaminated with sewage. Use your stored water first. When it runs out, treat any other water. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) gives these methods. If the water is cloudy, first let it settle and pour the clear part through a clean cloth.

items: **Boiling** (the safest method): bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, let it cool, and store it covered in a clean container.

**Household bleach**: use only plain, unscented liquid bleach whose label states the sodium hypochlorite strength. For bleach of 5 to 9%, add **2 drops per litre**. For 1% bleach, add **10 drops per litre**. Stir and let it stand for at least **30 minutes** before drinking. If you cannot find the strength on the label, do not guess: boil instead.
Disinfect a well or borehole only with guidance from your local government water or environmental health office.

blocks.title: Worked example: treating a jerrycan with bleach
blocks.context: For example, after a flood in Kogi, Zainab's stored water has run out. She has a 20-litre jerrycan of clear well water and a bottle of plain bleach labelled 5% sodium hypochlorite.
steps: She checks the label: plain, unscented, 5%. That falls in the 5 to 9% range, so the rule is 2 drops per litre.
Drops needed: 20 litres x 2 drops = 40 drops.
She adds 40 drops with a clean dropper, closes the jerrycan and shakes it gently.
She writes the time on the jerrycan and waits at least 30 minutes before anyone drinks.
For her baby's drinks she chooses boiled and cooled water.
blocks.result: 40 drops of 5% bleach in 20 litres, left for 30 minutes, gives water safe enough for drinking according to CDC emergency guidance.

blocks.title: Bleach safety
blocks.text: Never mix bleach with ammonia, acids or other cleaning products: it can release toxic gases. Store bleach out of children's reach, in its original labelled bottle, away from food and drinking water.
Food after a flood

Throw away any food that touched floodwater, unless it is in a sealed, undamaged tin. Also discard food in sacks, cartons, cellophane, or containers with screw caps or snap lids that were under water. Throw away food from a fridge or freezer that was without power long enough to warm up. Wash and disinfect pots, plates and cutting boards before use. The WHO "Five keys to safer food" apply strongly now: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials.

blocks.title: Watch for watery diarrhoea
blocks.text: Cholera and other diarrhoeal diseases often follow floods. If anyone has sudden watery diarrhoea or vomiting, start oral rehydration salts (ORS) mixed exactly as the sachet instructs, and take them to the nearest primary health centre or hospital at once. Sleep under a treated mosquito net, as standing water increases mosquitoes.
Psychological first aid: Look, Listen, Link

Disasters also wound people inside. The WHO guide **Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers** describes simple, humane support that anyone can give. **Look**: check for safety, for people with urgent needs, and for people showing serious distress. **Listen**: approach gently, ask about needs and concerns, and help people feel calm, without forcing them to talk. **Link**: help people get information, practical needs such as water or shelter, and connect them with loved ones and services. You are not a counsellor; you are a calm neighbour who listens and helps people find help.

blocks.name: medical-care
blocks.alt: A health worker caring for a person
blocks.caption: Link people with serious distress or injury to a health facility; your role is to listen and connect.

takeaways: Return in daylight when authorities say it is safe, check structure first, and keep power off until an electrician checks.
Photograph damage before cleaning or throwing anything away.
Boil water for 1 minute, or use 2 drops of 5 to 9% unscented bleach per litre and wait 30 minutes.
Discard food that touched floodwater unless in a sealed, undamaged tin.
Psychological first aid is Look, Listen and Link.

activity.title: Prepare your safe-return card
steps: Write the six safe-return steps on a card and put it in your grab bag.
Check the bleach in your home: is it plain and unscented, and what strength is printed on the label?
Work out how many drops you would need for your largest water container.
Write the name, location and phone number of your nearest primary health centre on the card.
Practise Look, Listen and Link with a friend using a short role play.
activity.evidence: A photo of the completed safe-return card with your bleach calculation and clinic details.

lessons.title: Recovering Income and Building Back Better
objectives: Record damage and losses in a way relief agencies and landlords accept
Build a simple recovery budget for a household or small business
Compare rebuilding as before with building back better
Identify savings, group and insurance options that speed up recovery

blocks.text: Recovery is not just cleaning. It is restarting income, replacing what was lost and, wherever possible, rebuilding in a way that will suffer less damage next time. The Sendai Framework calls this **Build Back Better**. For a household or small trader, it often means small, smart changes made at the moment you are rebuilding anyway.

blocks.name: house-building
blocks.caption: The moment of repair is the cheapest moment to make a home or shop safer.

blocks.text: Step 1: Record damage and losses

Relief agencies such as SEMA and NEMA usually register affected households during or after an event, often through community leaders or at camps. Having clear records makes registration easier and fairer. Keep one recovery folder with: photos and videos of damage with the date; a list of lost items with approximate value; copies of NIN and other documents; and the names of officials or volunteers you spoke to, with dates. Never pay anyone who asks for money to put your name on a relief list; report it to the agency.
Step 2: Build a recovery budget

blocks.title: Worked example: a trader's recovery budget
blocks.context: For example, Funmi sells provisions from a small shop in a flood-prone part of Lagos. Water entered the shop to about 40 cm. All prices below are approximate and only for illustration.
steps: Losses: stock on the floor and lowest shelf worth about N180,000, and a damaged chest freezer.
Money available: N60,000 in her emergency savings and N100,000 due to her from her ajo group next month.
Recovery needs: restock fast-moving goods N150,000, freezer repair N35,000, three metal shelves to raise stock N45,000. Total N150,000 + N35,000 + N45,000 = N230,000.
Gap: N230,000 needed minus N160,000 available = N70,000.
She restarts with the fast-moving goods first so cash flows again, asks a supplier for 2 weeks' credit on part of the restock, and delays the freezer repair until the ajo payout.
blocks.result: Funmi reopens within days with a clear N70,000 gap and a plan to cover it, instead of borrowing large sums from a lender at high interest in a panic.

blocks.text: A useful order for recovery spending is: first, anything needed for health and safety (safe water, medicines, urgent repairs that stop further damage); second, whatever restarts income fastest, such as fast-selling stock or tools for your trade; third, protection against the next event, such as raised shelves; and last, replacing comfort items. Income first does not mean ignoring the home. It means that once money is flowing again, every other repair becomes easier to pay for. Keep receipts for everything you buy during recovery, both for your own records and in case a relief or insurance claim asks for proof.

Women often lose more than goods in a disaster: land or tenancy papers held in a husband's or relative's name, stock bought on credit, and time spent caring for others instead of trading. When you list losses, include your business and any items you own or manage yourself, and keep copies of any agreement that shows your rights to land, a shop or a stall.

blocks.title: Beware of recovery scams
blocks.text: After disasters, fake relief agents, loan apps and "grant" messages appear. Real relief registration does not require you to pay a fee or share your bank PIN or OTP. Check any offer with your community leader, SEMA, or the organisation's official contact before giving information.
Step 3: Build back better

blocks.title: Rebuilding choices
items: Rebuild as before
Build back better
left: Sockets at the same low height
right: Stock on raised shelves above the flood mark
Sockets and meter raised by an electrician
Documents in waterproof bags, photos online
Drain cleared and kept clear by the street
blocks.caption: Most build-back-better choices cost little extra when done during repair.

head: Hazard
Build-back-better ideas for homes and small businesses
rows: Flood

Mark the highest water level on a wall and store goods above it; raise the floor or doorstep where possible; ask an electrician to raise sockets; use materials that dry out, such as tiles, at floor level
Fire
Replace damaged wiring rather than patching; do not overload extension boxes; keep gas cylinders outside or in a ventilated space; keep a sand bucket or extinguisher near the kitchen
Windstorm
Fix roofing sheets with enough nails or bolts and ask a roofer about strapping the roof to the walls; trim weak branches over the house
Drought
Add water storage and simple rainwater collection from the roof; keep a small food reserve bought when prices are lower

blocks.text: For structural work, always use a qualified builder. If you rent, discuss repairs and improvements with your landlord in writing before you spend money.
Step 4: Financial tools for faster recovery

items: **Emergency savings**: even a small weekly amount saved in a separate account or mobile money wallet builds a buffer.
**Savings groups**: ajo, esusu and cooperative groups can agree a rule to bring forward a payout for a member hit by disaster.

**Insurance**: some insurers offer cover for shops, stock and homes, and the Nigerian Agricultural Insurance Corporation offers farm cover. Check that any insurer is licensed by NAICOM (National Insurance Commission) and read what is and is not covered before paying.
**Document backups**: photos of NIN, certificates and land papers stored in a secure online account speed up replacement.

takeaways: Keep a recovery folder: dated photos, a loss list, document copies and names of officials.
A recovery budget shows the real gap so you can restart income first.
Build back better: raise stock, sockets and documents above flood level when repairing.
Never pay to be put on a relief list; check offers with official contacts.
Savings groups, emergency funds and NAICOM-licensed insurance speed recovery.

activity.title: Draft your recovery and build-back-better plan
steps: Start a recovery folder (paper or phone) with sections for photos, loss list, documents and contacts.
Mark on your wall or note in writing the highest level water or damage has reached in your home or shop.
List three build-back-better changes for your top hazard with an approximate cost for each.
Write a mini recovery budget: likely losses, money available, recovery needs and the gap.
Ask your savings group whether it has an emergency payout rule, and propose one if not.
activity.evidence: The recovery budget, the list of three build-back-better changes and a photo of your recovery folder.

lessons.title: Leading Community Readiness: Partnerships, Requests and Your 90-Day Plan
objectives: Map local partners who can support community preparedness
Write a specific, measurable request to a partner
Use local history to communicate risk persuasively
Plan and present a 90-day community readiness plan for your capstone

blocks.text: Household preparation protects your family. Community preparation protects the street, the market and the people who cannot prepare alone. You do not need a title to lead this. Many effective community efforts in Nigeria start with women's groups, market associations, faith groups and Community Development Associations (CDAs).

blocks.name: team-work
blocks.alt: A group of people working together
blocks.caption: Preparedness is stronger when households, leaders and agencies work as one.

blocks.text: Mapping your partners

head: Partner
What they may offer
How to approach
rows: LEMA or local emergency committee, local government
Alerts, evacuation support, relief registration, drain clearing
Visit the LGA secretariat or ask your ward councillor for the right desk officer
SEMA
State alerts, training, camps and relief in larger events
Use the official phone numbers or social media pages
Nigerian Red Cross Society local branch
First aid training and community volunteers
Contact the state branch office
Ward councillor, traditional and religious leaders
Influence, meeting spaces, announcements
Request a short slot at an existing meeting
CDA, market association, women's and youth groups
People, labour for drain clearing, phone tree captains
Present your hazard ranking and ask for one specific commitment
Primary health centre
Health talks, outbreak alerts, first aid
Ask the officer in charge for a short session

blocks.text: Making a specific request

Partners respond to requests that are clear, small and measurable. Compare "Please help us with disasters" with "Our street committee has 60 households on the river side of Ward 4. We have trained 5 phone tree captains. We ask LEMA to add our warning lead to its alert list and to send someone for a one-hour flood safety talk at the school on a Saturday in May." The second request names who, what, how many and when, and shows you have already started.

blocks.title: Worked example: from one household to a street
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in a riverside ward of Lokoja finished Modules 1 and 2 and wants to extend the work to her street of 40 households.
steps: She presents her hazard ranking and the neighbours' memories of past floods at the monthly women's group meeting, using the flood mark on the old mosque wall as proof.
Twelve women agree to do the 40-point audit at home; the average score is 13 of 40, or 33%.
The CDA agrees to two drain-clearing days before the rains, with 20 youths each day.
She writes to the LGA asking for the warning lead to be added to the alert list and for a flood safety talk.
After 90 days, 22 of 40 households (55%) have a written plan, the phone tree reaches everyone in 15 minutes, and the average audit score is 24 of 40 (60%).
blocks.result: Hauwa's street moved from 33% to 60% average readiness, with measured results she can show to partners when asking for more support.

blocks.text: Communicating risk so people act

items: Use local evidence: past flood marks, the year an event happened, names of streets affected. Real memory moves people more than general warnings.
Speak the language people use at home and use voice notes for those who do not read.
Always pair a warning with a simple action: "Put your documents in a zip bag this week".
Share progress: "Last month 8 households had plans; now 22 do" encourages others to join.

blocks.text: Running a short community meeting

Keep meetings to 45 minutes and use an existing gathering where possible, such as a women's group, a CDA meeting or after a religious service. A simple agenda works well: five minutes on why (a past local event and this year's outlook), ten minutes on what households can do (kit, plan, drill), fifteen minutes on the community idea you want support for, ten minutes for questions, and five minutes to write down names of volunteers and the next date. Bring a printed or hand-written sign-up sheet. Ask a respected elder or leader to open the meeting; their support signals that the effort is serious. Afterwards, send a short WhatsApp summary or voice note to everyone who attended with the agreed actions, names and dates, so nothing depends on memory.
Your 90-day community readiness plan

blocks.title: A 90-day readiness plan
items: Days 1 to 15: map and meet
Days 16 to 45: audits and kits
Days 46 to 75: phone tree and drill
Days 76 to 90: review and report
blocks.caption: Each phase ends with something you can count, so progress is visible to everyone.

blocks.text: Write your plan with three columns: **action**, **who**, **by when**, plus one measurable target for each phase. Keep it realistic for your time. A plan that 15 households complete fully is worth more than a big plan that stops after two weeks.

blocks.title: Preparing your capstone
blocks.text: Your capstone pulls together everything from this course: your hazard ranking, audit before and after, kit and grab bag photos, one-page plan and drill record, one community activity with its results, and your 90-day plan. Keep each item dated.
Finally, look after yourself. Leading others through risk can be tiring and sometimes upsetting. Share the work with a co-lead, and celebrate each step your community completes.

takeaways: Partners include LEMA, SEMA, the Red Cross, ward leaders, CDAs, faith groups and the health centre.
Specific requests name who, what, how many and when, and show work already done.
Local evidence and a simple action make risk messages work.
A 90-day plan has phases, owners, dates and measurable targets.

activity.title: Draft your partner request and 90-day plan
steps: List at least four local partners with a contact person or office for each.
Write one specific request to one partner, naming who, what, how many and when.
Draft your 90-day plan with four phases, actions, owners, dates and one target per phase.
Present the plan at one existing community meeting and record who agreed to help.
Book the date for your first community activity.
activity.evidence: The written request, the 90-day plan and a list of people who agreed to take part.

quiz.q: Floodwater has gone down and Joy wants to move back home. Which step comes first?
options: Switch on the mains to check the lights
Wait for the all-clear, return in daylight and check the building from outside
Drink well water to save stored water
quiz.explain: Return only when authorities say it is safe, in daylight, and check for structural damage from outside before entering. Power stays off until an electrician checks.

quiz.q: Mary has a 10-litre container of clear water and plain unscented bleach labelled 6%. How many drops should she add?
quiz.explain: For 5 to 9% bleach, use 2 drops per litre: 10 x 2 = 20 drops, then wait at least 30 minutes.

quiz.q: Which food can be kept after it was under floodwater?
options: A sealed, undamaged tin, washed and disinfected before opening
Groundnut oil in a bottle with a screw cap
quiz.explain: Only sealed, undamaged tins can be kept and cleaned. Sacks, cartons and screw-cap containers let floodwater in.

quiz.q: Funmi's recovery needs total N250,000 (approximate) and she has N190,000 available. What is her gap?
quiz.explain: 250,000 - 190,000 = 60,000. Knowing the exact gap lets her plan supplier credit or timing instead of panic borrowing.

quiz.q: A man calls Halima saying he can add her name to the flood relief list for a fee of N5,000. What should she do?
options: Pay quickly before the list closes
Send her BVN and OTP to confirm
Refuse, and report it to her community leader or SEMA
Pay half now and half later
quiz.explain: Genuine relief registration does not charge a fee. Requests for payment or OTPs are signs of a scam.

quiz.q: Which request to LEMA is most likely to get a useful response?
options: "We need everything you can give us."
"Our 60 riverside households have trained phone tree captains; please add our warning lead to your alert list and give a one-hour flood talk in May."
"Why did you not warn us last year?"
quiz.explain: Specific requests that name who, what, how many and when, and show work already done, are easier for a partner to say yes to.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement best describes disaster risk?
options: It depends only on how strong the hazard is
It grows with hazard, exposure and vulnerability and shrinks with capacity
It cannot be changed by households
It is the same for everyone in a town
finalQuiz.explain: Risk combines the hazard with exposure and vulnerability, and is reduced by capacity such as plans, kits and savings.

finalQuiz.q: Ijeoma's community floods most years. Which official publication lists LGAs by flood risk each year?
finalQuiz.explain: The Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency publishes the Annual Flood Outlook, which names states and LGAs by risk level.

finalQuiz.q: Drought scores likelihood 3 and impact 3; fire scores likelihood 2 and impact 4. Which has the higher priority score?
options: Fire, because fire is always first
finalQuiz.explain: 3 x 3 = 9 for drought and 2 x 4 = 8 for fire, so drought ranks slightly higher for this household.

finalQuiz.q: A household audit scored 14 of 40 in March and 30 of 40 in June. By how many percentage points did readiness rise?
How much water should a family of 4 store for 3 days at 4 litres per person per day?
finalQuiz.explain: 4 people x 4 litres x 3 days = 48 litres.

finalQuiz.q: Which item belongs in the grab bag rather than only in the home kit?
options: Sealed copies of NIN slips and land papers with a paper phone list
finalQuiz.explain: The grab bag is small and portable. Document copies and a paper contact list are essential if you must leave quickly.

finalQuiz.q: During a power cut Amaka wants to run the generator. Where should it go?
options: In the corridor with the door open
Inside the shop to keep it safe from thieves
Outdoors, well away from doors and windows
In the kitchen next to an open window
finalQuiz.explain: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which you cannot see or smell and which can kill. Run it outdoors, away from openings.

finalQuiz.q: A grandmother in the household walks slowly with a stick. What should the plan include?
options: She stays behind to guard the house
She leaves last after everyone else
Nothing extra, the general plan covers her
A named helper and a back-up, with her shoes and stick kept by her bed
finalQuiz.explain: Inclusion means planning person by person: named helpers and practical preparations for anyone who needs help to move.

finalQuiz.q: Which is one of the four elements of a people-centred early warning system?
finalQuiz.explain: The four elements are risk knowledge, monitoring and forecasting, warning dissemination and communication, and preparedness to respond.

finalQuiz.q: Ronke has a 25-litre container of clear water and plain unscented 5% bleach. How many drops does she add and how long does she wait?
finalQuiz.explain: For 5 to 9% bleach, 2 drops per litre: 25 x 2 = 50 drops, then wait at least 30 minutes.

finalQuiz.q: While repairing her flooded shop, Comfort can choose one change. Which is a build-back-better choice?
options: Put stock back on the floor to save time
Fit raised shelves above the highest flood mark
Keep documents in the same low drawer
finalQuiz.explain: Raising stock above the known flood level reduces future losses at little extra cost during repair.

finalQuiz.q: A distressed neighbour is sitting alone after losing her shop. Using psychological first aid, what should Patience do?
options: Insist she describes everything that happened
Tell her to stop crying and be strong
Leave her alone until she asks for help
Approach calmly, listen to her needs, and link her to practical help and family
finalQuiz.explain: WHO psychological first aid is Look, Listen and Link: notice needs, listen without forcing, and connect people to help and loved ones.

capstone.title: Household and Community Disaster Readiness Project
capstone.brief: Produce a dated readiness file showing your household fully prepared for its top hazard and one measured community preparedness effort: hazard ranking, before-and-after audit, kit and grab bag, tested plan, a community activity with results, a recovery folder and a 90-day plan to extend readiness to more households.
steps: Rank your hazards with likelihood x impact scores using official outlooks and at least two community interviews.
Complete the 40-point audit at the start, record the percentage, and fix your gaps in order.
Assemble the home kit and grab bag with a written water and food calculation and a dated kit list.
Write your one-page household plan, run two timed drills and record the improvement.
Lead one community activity: a phone tree test, a drain-clearing day, a vulnerable-residents helper list, or a partner request to LEMA or SEMA, and record its results.
Set up your recovery folder with document backups, a safe-return card and three build-back-better changes.
Repeat the audit, compare scores, and write a 90-day plan with phases, owners, dates and targets.
evidence: Hazard ranking table and interview notes
Before and after audit sheets with percentages
Photos of the home kit and grab bag with the dated kit list
Signed one-page plan and drill record with both times
Community activity record: phone tree chart, timed test, attendance or partner letter and reply
Safe-return card with your bleach calculation and clinic details
